titulo.texto: Funerary Bundle from the Candelaria Cave

frase_gancho.texto: A bundle of blankets and cords that the desert preserved for centuries.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the bundle, we move on to one specific person. Look for an elongated skull that still keeps its headdress of cords dyed red.

guion_corto.texto: This bundle, about eighty-five centimeters tall, comes from the Candelaria Cave in Coahuila, and it was made between the years 1000 and 1300 AD. It is a funerary bundle: a person with the body bent, in a fetal position, wrapped in several layers of mats and blankets made of yucca and agave fibers, and tied with cords. Everything was woven by hand, without a loom. Take a look at the textiles and the cords: in a very dry cave, organic material hardly rots, and that is why sandals, baskets, and other everyday objects were preserved as well. They are simple things, but they speak of great care for the dead.

guion_largo.texto:
There are places where time stands still, and the Candelaria Cave, in the mountain range of the same name, in Coahuila, is one of them. It is so dry that what is left there hardly rots: not the fabrics, not the cords, not the sandals, not even the hair. That is why we know, today, objects that almost anywhere else in Mexico would have vanished within a few years.

Think of the Maya in the Maya Hall. Their clothing, their paper books, and their wooden furniture were almost completely lost in the humidity of the jungle; what remains of them is mostly stone, clay, and jade. Here the opposite happened: the desert kept precisely what is fragile. Each region preserves a different part of history, and you have to visit them all to get the complete picture.

The groups that used this cave were hunters and gatherers. They returned to it to bury their dead, and that is why many bundles have been found in the same place, one beside another. In the mid-twentieth century, the INAH explored it and recovered numerous pieces. It was, in a way, a family cemetery sheltered by the rock. Imagine what that means: a group that walked great distances and came back to the same place to bid farewell to their loved ones. The dead were a reason to return.

Look at the textiles slowly. They did not use a loom. With their hands they braided, knotted, and interlaced fibers of lechuguilla, yucca, and agave, desert plants that give a very strong thread, called ixtle. Making a blanket like this demanded enormous patience. When you reach the Upper Floor, you will see the other great weaving system of Mexico, the backstrap loom, and you will understand where so much skill comes from.

The posture of the body is no accident either. In many places around the world, a person is buried bent over, as they were before being born, and it has been thought that this is a way of understanding death as a return. The Mexica, according to the chronicles, also wrapped their dead in blankets and tied them in a seated position. The hands and the desert change, but the idea of wrapping up the one who departs is very similar.

Beside the dead person, everyday things were left: wicker sandals, bags, stone tools, bows and arrows, and sometimes the spear-thrower you already saw in the hands of the [Tula atlantean](mna_s05_atlante_tula). There is no gold or jade. If you compare it with the grave goods of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán or with the [tomb of Pakal](mna_s09_cripta_pakal), the difference is plain to see. And yet the gesture is the same: no one should leave without what they need for the journey.

It is not a mummy like those of Egypt, which were prepared with elaborate techniques. Here, what preserved the body and the textiles was mostly the dry air of the cave. The desert did the work. It is a reminder that these peoples, whom we sometimes call simply nomads, had complex rituals, family memory, and great manual skill.

texto: Follow the cords that tie the bundle and look at how they are braided
Look for the layers of mats and blankets, one over another
Imagine the sandals and the objects that accompanied the deceased

texto.Material: Woven plant fibers (yucca, lechuguilla and cotton)

texto.pregunta: Myth: This bundle is an embalmed mummy, like those of Egypt.
texto.respuesta: Reality: What preserved the body and the textiles was mostly the dryness of the cave. The desert did the work.
